Acquisition, Retention, Monetisation Actions

What actions turn a visitor into a user, a user into a returning user, and a returning user into revenue?

1. A Tuesday in Gurugram

On the morning of 15 September 2026, Meera Chandrasekaran, senior product manager for growth at Ekatra Fresh, a fifteen-minute grocery delivery startup, sat in the Gurugram office with a board deck due in six days. Ekatra Fresh operated forty dark stores across Delhi NCR, Pune and Hyderabad, competing for the same wallet as Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, on a monthly cash burn of ₹4.2 crore. Its board, led by an investor who had watched three quick-commerce companies fold in the last eighteen months, had given Meera one instruction for the next fundraise: show that the money spent brings back users who stay and pay, not just users who download.

The problem was that Ekatra Fresh's dashboard told three unrelated stories. Marketing reported 118,000 app installs in August. Data science reported that "monthly active users" had grown 9%. Finance reported that revenue per order had fallen for the third month running. Nobody could say which number, if any, should change how the next ₹1.5 crore of growth budget was spent. Vikram Rao, Ekatra's data lead in Bengaluru, put it bluntly on the call: "We are measuring everything and deciding nothing." Meera's task before the board meeting was to rebuild the story around three questions any investor would ask — who becomes a user, who stays, and who pays — and to prove each with a countable action, not a vibe.

2. The idea

Acquisition, Retention and Monetisation actions — ARM — are the three families of user behaviour a product must generate, in that order, for a business to exist. An acquisition action is the specific, observable step by which a visitor becomes a counted user: not "awareness," but the exact event — a completed sign-up, a first verified order — a company logs as the moment someone joined. A retention action is the step by which a user returns and behaves like a user again, inside a defined window: a second order within fourteen days, a weekly login. A monetisation action is the step by which a returning user converts into revenue: a paid order, a subscription renewal. ARM is deliberately a taxonomy of actions, not metrics — a metric is a rate computed from an action once you decide what to count and over what window.

ARM is the action layer of GAME, the broader discipline that asks a team to pick Goals, define the Actions that serve them, choose Metrics that count those actions, and set an Evaluation cadence. ARM narrows GAME's "actions" step to the funnel a growth team runs, organising actions by which stage of the user's life with the product they belong to. The framework has no single named inventor; it crystallised through the 2000s and 2010s as consumer internet companies — most visibly the growth teams around Dave McClure's 500 Startups cohort circa 2007 — needed a shared vocabulary simpler than a full funnel model before a board meeting. ARM is usually taught as the coarse, three-bucket version a team reaches for first, before splitting into the five-stage AARRR ("pirate metrics") model that separates activation and referral out from acquisition and retention.

The sentence Meera could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "Every rupee we spend either creates an acquisition action, a retention action or a monetisation action — and if I can't name which one, I can't tell you if it worked."

3. How it actually works

Building an ARM view is not a data-science exercise; it is a naming exercise followed by an arithmetic one, and most teams skip the naming.

Step 1 — name one action per stage, in the past tense of a log line

Meera's first move was to reject "installs," "active users" and "revenue" as starting points, because none of them is a single event a database can log. She replaced them with three sentences an engineer could turn into an event name: Acquisition — "user completed sign-up and placed one verified order within 24 hours" (event: first_order_verified). Retention — "a previously acquired user placed a second order within 14 days of the first" (event: second_order_in_14d). Monetisation — "an order closed with Ekatra Fresh's margin (item margin plus delivery fee minus discount) positive" (event: margin_positive_order). This is where practitioners usually skip implicit work: choosing the time window (14 days, not 7 or 30) and the qualifying condition (verified, not just attempted) is a judgement call that determines every number that follows, and it has to be written down, not left to whoever built the dashboard first.

Step 2 — assign an owner, a cadence and a decision to each action

An action without an owner decays into a chart nobody reads. Meera assigned the acquisition action to Ananya Bhatt, performance marketing lead in Mumbai, reviewed weekly, feeding "which channel gets next week's budget." The retention action went to Farhan Qureshi, lifecycle product manager in Pune, reviewed weekly, feeding "which cohort gets a re-engagement push." The monetisation action went to Meera herself, reviewed monthly, feeding "which categories get commission renegotiated with dark-store partners." Three actions, three owners, three cadences, three decisions — the discipline that turns a metrics tree from decoration into an operating system.

Step 3 — instrument the funnel so one user can be traced through all three

The events had to share a user ID so the same person's three rows could be joined. Vikram's team in Bengaluru spent four days closing gaps where the app's install SDK and the order-management system used different identifiers — unglamorous but load-bearing, since ARM is worthless if acquisition and retention are counted on incompatible cohorts.

Step 4 — compute rates, not just counts, and set a target for each

Counts answer "how many"; rates answer "how well." Meera's team computed acquisition rate (visitors to first_order_verified), a 14-day retention rate (acquired users to second_order_in_14d), and a monetisation rate (retained users to margin_positive_order), each with a target the team could be held to.

4. The arithmetic, walked through

Of 118,000 app visits in August, 9,440 completed first_order_verified: an acquisition rate of 8.0%. Of those, 2,832 placed a second order within fourteen days: a retention rate of 30%. Of those 2,832 retained users, 2,265 produced a margin-positive order in the same window: a monetisation rate of 80%. Multiply the three rates and 19.2% of every visitor became a paying, returning customer within the month. At an average order margin of ₹38, that cohort was worth about ₹8.6 lakh, against acquisition spend of ₹340 per acquired user, or ₹32.1 lakh for the 9,440 acquisitions. On these numbers alone, the growth spend looked underwater.

Now change one input. Farhan's Pune team ran a WhatsApp reminder nudging users toward their second order on day nine instead of leaving it to chance; retention rose from 30% to 39%, with acquisition and monetisation held constant. Retained users rose to 3,682; monetised users to 2,946; monthly margin from that cohort rose to roughly ₹11.2 lakh, a 30% lift, for a nudge campaign costing under ₹2 lakh to build. Acquisition spend did not change at all — the same 9,440 acquired users simply converted more efficiently. This is the arithmetic case for why Meera's board slide led with retention, not the install number marketing had been proud of.

5. Nuances a learner must catch

Acquisition is not activation

ARM's buckets are coarse on purpose. "Acquisition" here quietly bundles two things — installing the app and doing something valuable in it — into one action. The finer distinction, which the fuller AARRR model draws out, separates "signed up" from "reached the aha moment." Treating them as one, as Ekatra Fresh initially did, hides whether the 8.0% conversion problem is a marketing problem or a first-order-experience problem.

An action is not a metric

The action is what you log (second_order_in_14d); the metric is the rate you compute from it. Confusing the two lets teams "improve the metric" by changing the definition rather than changing behaviour — widening the window from 14 to 30 days lifts the rate without anyone doing anything differently.

The time window is a decision, not a fact

There is no natural law that retention means "within 14 days." A grocery app and an annual tax-filing app need different windows because the rhythm of the underlying need differs. Picking the window before looking at the data, and defending why, is part of the job; picking it after, to make a number look better, is the most common form of ARM malpractice.

Monetisation actions are not always purchases

For an ad-supported or freemium product, the monetisation action might be "watched a rewarded ad to completion," not a transaction at all. Teams that assume monetisation always means "bought something" misdiagnose free products as having no monetisation funnel, when they simply have a different qualifying event.

One user occupies multiple roles at once

A single customer can simultaneously be a retention action for this month and a monetisation action for this order; ARM is three counters the same person can trigger repeatedly, not a life-stage label stamped on once. "Our retained users" spoken of as a fixed segment, rather than a rate recomputed each period, misrepresents this.

Vanity actions masquerade as real ones

An action must tie to value delivered, not merely usage. "Opened the app" is easy to log and easy to inflate with push notifications. The test: if a bot faking the action would still make the business look like it succeeded, it is a vanity action.

ARM cannot tell you why

Even perfectly instrumented, ARM answers "what happened," not "why." A retention rate that fell from 35% to 30% could be a competitor's price cut, a stockout, or an app crash; ARM shows the drop but never explains it, so it must sit beside qualitative research and experiments, not replace them.

The three rates are not independent

Loosening the acquisition qualifying bar (say, counting an unverified order as acquired) will mechanically depress the retention rate, because the denominator now includes lower-intent users. A team that "improves" acquisition while retention falls has often just moved the same weak signups across a boundary, not created new value — always check whether an ARM number moved because behaviour changed or because a definition changed.

6. How it differs by context

In a consumer app like Ekatra Fresh, all three ARM actions happen inside days, driven mostly by product and marketing. In a B2B product, the same actions can span months: "acquisition" might be a signed pilot, "retention" a renewed seat count at the next billing cycle, "monetisation" an expansion order — each owned by a different function (sales, customer success, account management), reviewed quarterly not weekly. In a marketplace, ARM runs twice, once per side: a partner's "acquisition" (listing live), "retention" (still fulfilling after 60 days) and "monetisation" (commission paid) sit alongside the same actions for shoppers, and the two funnels interact — a fall in partner retention shows up two weeks later as a fall in shopper monetisation, because stockouts push shoppers to competitors. Stage matters too: an early-stage team treats ARM as a story for investors, trusting only monthly numbers; a large, mature company runs it per city, per category, per cohort, with automated alerts rather than a weekly stare at a dashboard.

7. Common mistakes

Reporting counts instead of rates. Symptom: a board slide says "150,000 installs, up 20%" with no mention of what fraction did anything afterward. Misunderstanding: counts feel more impressive and are easier to produce than rates. Diagnostic: ask "up 20% of what denominator, and did the denominator also move?" — if nobody can answer instantly, the number is decoration.

No owner for the middle action. Symptom: acquisition and monetisation are reviewed weekly, retention "whenever someone remembers." Misunderstanding: retention is treated as a lagging outcome of the other two rather than an action with its own levers. Diagnostic: ask who was in the room the last time the retention number moved by more than two points — if the answer is "nobody," there is no owner.

Redefining the window after the fact. Symptom: the retention window quietly changes from 14 to 30 days the same month the rate would otherwise have dropped below target. Misunderstanding: treating the definition as a lever to pull rather than a fixed measuring stick. Diagnostic: check the definition's last-changed date against the trend line — a change that coincides with an inflection is a red flag, not a coincidence.

Conflating acquisition efficiency with product quality. Symptom: CAC looks healthy, but monetisation per retained user is falling, and leadership still calls the funnel "working." Misunderstanding: acquisition is the most visible, most fundable action, so teams over-index on it. Diagnostic: compute the blended ARM rate (acquisition × retention × monetisation) monthly and watch whether one stage is carrying the others while they quietly erode.

8. What good looks like

Six weeks later, the same three-stage story appeared on Ekatra Fresh's board slide, but every number had an owner's name next to it and a note on what changed it: the 9-day WhatsApp nudge, attributable and costed. Ananya's acquisition rate held at 8.0% with CAC unchanged. Farhan's retention rate sat at 39%, with a named experiment behind the gain and a next test already running. Meera's monetisation rate held at 80%, and she could say precisely which two categories carried the lowest margin per order and were up for commission renegotiation. The investor asked one question — "which of these three would you protect first if you had to cut the growth budget by a third?" — and Meera answered without hesitation: retention, the only stage where a rupee had already been shown, with real numbers, to move monetisation two stages downstream.

9. What Meera decided, and what comes next

Meera's board slide shifted ₹60 lakh of the next quarter's growth budget from acquisition channels toward retention: two more lifecycle engineers and a loyalty pilot in Pune and Hyderabad, funded by trimming a paid-social channel whose users retained at half the organic rate. The reasoning was the ARM logic itself: acquisition without retention buys installs that evaporate, retention without monetisation buys loyal users who cost more than they return, but a rupee spent lifting retention compounds through monetisation every month that follows. The natural next stop is the fuller AARRR framework, which splits "acquisition" into acquisition and activation and adds referral as a fourth engine — the categories ARM's coarse first bucket was quietly hiding. From there, constructing a funnel and precisely defining activation's "aha moment" turn these three broad buckets into a diagram with real conversion rates at every step, the tool Meera will need the next time a single stage has to explain a shortfall to the board.

Two questions to sit with: First, for a product you use daily, what is the exact event its team probably logs as your "retention action" — and what time window would make that definition either generous or strict? Second, when a company reports one headline growth number, which of the three ARM stages is it most likely hiding a weakness in, and why would that be the easiest one to leave out of the slide?

Acquisition, Retention, Monetisation Actions

What actions turn a visitor into a user, a user into a returning user, and a returning user into revenue — and why the three are not the independent levers the diagram suggests.

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On the evening of 8 September 2026, Rukmini Iyer, head of growth at Ankahi, sat in the company's Lower Parel office in Mumbai with a test readout she did not want to present. Ankahi published long-form audio fiction in Hindi, Marathi and Bengali — the audio equivalent of the pocket novels sold at railway stalls. It had 41 lakh monthly listeners, ₹1.9 crore a month in programmatic advertising and ₹1.2 crore from Ankahi Khazana, a ₹149 subscription that removed ads and unlocked completed series, against a burn of ₹2.4 crore.

The test was a hard paywall on the Marathi catalogue: three free episodes per series, then a wall. Every monetisation number improved — trial starts rose from 2.1% of weekly actives to 5.4%. Every other number fell. Day-30 retention of new installs dropped from 22% to 16%, and ad impressions per retained listener fell 31%, because the listeners who stayed were disproportionately the ones who had paid and saw no ads. Leadership met on 30 September to decide on a national rollout. The chief executive had already called the test "monetisation up 2.5x" on WhatsApp, and Rukmini's problem was that this was true, arithmetically, and told nobody anything useful.

In Bengaluru, on 11 September, Arvind Menon faced a different version of the same question. Arvind was chief product officer of Bandobast Systems, which sold a distributor-management platform to mid-market manufacturers — paint, cement and packaged-food firms reaching retailers through two hundred–odd distributors each, a channel historically run on WhatsApp and Tally exports. Bandobast had ₹46 crore of recurring revenue across 310 customers, gross revenue retention of 88% and net revenue retention of 104% against a board target of 120%.

Bandobast's dashboard reported weekly active seats, and they were healthy: 71% of licensed seats logged in each week. Yet three of the four customers who had churned in two quarters — including Chirag Coatings, a ₹19 lakh account — had shown seat activity above 70% in the month before giving notice. Prachi Dubey, who ran customer success from Noida, said the uncomfortable thing on the Monday call: "They log in to check what the distributor already sent us on WhatsApp. That is a second screen, not usage." Arvind's question was not how to improve retention, but whether the action he had called retention for three years was the right action at all.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Acquisition, retention and monetisation actions — ARM — is the discipline of naming, for a product, the three user behaviours that bring a person in, bring them back, and turn their presence into revenue. The unit is the action, not the metric. An ARM action is a logged event with five properties fixed in advance: identity grain, qualifying condition, time window, counting basis, and an owner with a cadence and a named decision. Strip one and you have a chart, not an action.

ARM is GAME's action layer — Goals, Actions, Metrics, Evaluation — narrowed to the growth funnel. Its ancestry predates software: the sequential funnel from advertising, in E. St Elmo Lewis's AIDA model of 1898; scoring customers by behaviour rather than demographics from catalogue retail's RFM analysis; cohort survival analysis from telecom churn modelling. The streams converged in late-2000s growth practice, crystallised in Dave McClure's 2007 "pirate metrics" (AARRR), with Ries's engines of growth and Croll and Yoskovitz's Lean Analytics carrying it into startups.

The problem it solves is specific: before ARM, product and marketing arguments ran on nouns — "awareness", "engagement", "loyalty" — which cannot be logged, owned or falsified. ARM forces each into a past-tense verb a database row can witness. Four schools disagree on what follows.

The stage-separability school, descended from McClure, holds that growth decomposes into a product of stage conversion rates, each ownable by a different team. It would sign: "Revenue equals visitors times acquisition times retention times monetisation times revenue per monetised user, and each factor is a legitimate independent target." It would not sign that retention deserves permanent primacy.

The retention-first school — Reichheld's loyalty economics, Ries's sticky engine, Sean Ellis's product-market-fit heuristics — holds that retention is not a stage but a state variable determining whether the other two mean anything. It would sign: "If the retention curve does not flatten to a non-zero asymptote, no acquisition spend creates a business, and monetisation merely accelerates extraction from a depleting stock." It would not sign that the three rates are interchangeable multiplicands.

The unit-economics school, from subscription finance, holds that ARM actions matter only as predictors of discounted contribution margin per cohort. It would sign: "An action whose correlation with cohort contribution margin has never been measured is decoration, however carefully instrumented." It would not sign that a retention action has value in itself.

The penetration school is the awkward guest. Drawing on Ehrenberg and Byron Sharp — double jeopardy, the negative-binomial distribution of buying, brands growing by adding light buyers rather than deepening heavy ones — it holds that the funnel is a reporting artefact imposing a false causal order on users who simply have episodes of need. It would sign: "Most incremental growth comes from acquiring light, infrequent users, and loyalty budgets are systematically misallocated." It would not sign that retention is the highest-leverage lever for everyone.

These are not four flavours of one opinion. A practitioner who cannot say which of the four they are arguing from is arguing from none of them.

3. Mechanics in depth

What separates a competent implementation from an expert one lies in the steps skipped because they look like paperwork.

The five fixings

Identity grain. Ankahi logs against a device until sign-in and an account afterwards, so acquisition numbers and retention numbers are computed on different populations. Bandobast's version is sharper: retention is a behaviour of users, monetisation a behaviour of accounts, and one account holds between 4 and 180 users. Arvind's dashboard averaged a user-grain rate and an account-grain rate into one "health" number — a category error dressed as an average.

Qualifying condition. "Installed" is not an acquisition action; "completed a listening session of at least five minutes within 24 hours of install" is. The bar belongs at the earliest point where the user has done the economically meaningful thing and no earlier, because earlier is cheap to hit and predicts nothing.

Window. Derive it from the rhythm of the need, not the calendar: take the median inter-event gap among users who event twice, double it, and confirm against the hazard curve, where the probability of returning stops falling steeply. For Ankahi that gave nine days; for Bandobast's distributors, 34, because order cycles are monthly.

Counting basis. A rolling 28-day active count and a cohort day-28 retention rate answer different questions and move in opposite directions during a growth spurt: rolling counts flatter fast-growing products.

Owner, cadence, decision. At Ankahi, acquisition belonged to performance marketing weekly against channel budget; retention to Devansh Puri's lifecycle team in Pune, weekly, against catalogue scheduling; monetisation to Sneha Kulkarni in Indore, monthly, against paywall and pricing.

The formal treatment, and where it misleads

The standard arithmetic is a product: cohort revenue equals visitors times acquisition rate a, retention rate r, monetisation rate m, and revenue per monetised user. Being multiplicative, a one-percent relative gain in any factor gives a one-percent gain in the total. The three rates are perfectly symmetric, so any preference between them must come from cost per point, not leverage.

That symmetry is real and also the source of the commonest expert-level error, because it holds only for a single-period funnel. Once revenue repeats, retention stops entering linearly: if a retained user generates margin M per period and survives each period with probability r, the expected number of paying periods is 1/(1−r), convex in r. At r = 0.70 a user is worth 3.33 periods; at 0.80, five; at 0.90, ten. The same five-point gain buys 0.8 periods at the low end and 2.5 at the high end.

The second-order effects experts price in

Three matter most. Denominator transfer: loosening an acquisition condition moves low-intent users across a boundary, mechanically raising acquisition and lowering retention with no behaviour change. Cannibalisation of organic return: a nudge raising fourteen-day retention may merely have pulled forward a visit due on day nineteen. The lagged cost of monetisation pressure: paywalls, ad-load increases and dunning campaigns depress retention a cycle or two later, after the readout was declared a success.

4. When the framework applies, and when it misleads

Three testable conditions govern whether ARM's stage logic fits.

One: the stages are separable in time. Ankahi passes — install, return, subscribe are days apart and ordered. Bandobast fails interestingly: the monetisation action, the contract, precedes acquisition of the actual users by two months, because a chief executive signs before any distributor logs in. Arvind's team ran ARM as two interleaved ledgers, one for buying and one for using.

Two: the rates are weakly coupled. The multiplicative form assumes moving one rate does not move another. Ankahi's paywall falsifies this: monetisation rose 2.5x because of a change that cut retention six points. Where coupling is strong, independent stage targets produce a team that hits every target while the business shrinks.

Three: value accrues per user, not per network. Where value depends on the population rather than the individual — marketplaces, social products, standards — a per-user ledger misprices both the first thousand users and the last.

Two situations make the framework actively misleading. In low-frequency, high-value categories — home loans, wedding services, capital purchases — the retention action may occur once in seven years, and insisting on a rate means measuring something irrelevant to justify the framework. And where usage carries a variable cost, the defining feature of AI-native products, retention and margin can move in opposite directions, so the assumption that more retention is better simply fails.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product. When an existing customer adopts a second product, is that acquisition or monetisation? Both are defensible; mature practice logs both in separate ledgers and never adds them, because adding double-counts the same person and produces an "acquisition" number that grows when nobody new arrives.

Two-sided. Bidri Bazaar, a handicrafts marketplace sourcing from Bidar and Moradabad, runs two ledgers with a coupling term. Its binding constraint is supply retention: when artisan 90-day retention fell from 61% to 48% after a commission change, buyer monetisation fell five weeks later as the catalogue thinned. The binding stage is rarely on the side that shows in the revenue line.

Regulated. Chukta Credit, a lending app working with a partner NBFC under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework, cannot log its own monetisation action: disbursal and interest accrual sit in the lender's system, and the Key Fact Statement and cooling-off period insert a mandatory delay. Regulated products routinely have one ARM action they do not own, reconciled daily against a partner's file.

Hardware plus software. Bindu Devices sells a connected water purifier at ₹12,900 plus a ₹399 monthly filter subscription. Acquisition is a point-of-sale transaction, retention is device telemetry, monetisation a recurring mandate in a billing system: three events, three systems, three organisations, no shared identity until somebody builds one.

AI-native. Chintan AI sells a contract-review copilot to Indian legal teams at ₹1,999 per seat per month; its heaviest retained users cost ₹2,400 a month in inference, so retaining them destroys value. Chintan redefined its monetisation action from "renewed" to "converted overage into a paid plan upgrade within 30 days", because in AI products that action is what stops retention becoming a liability.

At the organisational seams. Marketing owns acquisition, product retention, finance monetisation, and the two actions falling between owners are the two that rot: activation, and involuntary churn — failed autopay mandates, expired tokenised cards, UPI e-mandate debits never retried. Involuntary churn is usually the largest unowned leak, and it is invisible on an ARM dashboard because a user whose payment failed looks identical to one who left.

6. Nine nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Aggregate retention rises on its own. When a cohort mixes committed and casual users, the weak churn first, so survivors are progressively more committed and the period-over-period rate climbs though no individual's behaviour changed. In a cohort of 1,000 where 600 retain monthly at 50% and 400 at 90%, month-one retention is 66%, month two 71.8%, month three 77.3%. The tell is a curve that flattens and then bends upward exactly where the team claims credit for a fix; the correct reading is a mixture effect, formally a heterogeneity model such as the shifted-beta-geometric. "Our improvements are compounding" is wrong about as often as it is right.

A rate that improves while its denominator shrinks is usually bad news. Cut a poorly converting channel and acquisition rises, retention rises, and absolute users fall. Experts never read an ARM rate without the count beside it.

The window is a hypothesis about the user's life. Choosing fourteen days rather than thirty claims something about how often the need recurs. An expert can state the median inter-event gap that justified it; malpractice announces itself as a window that changed in the month the trend would otherwise have broken a target.

Monetisation is not always a purchase. For Ankahi's free tier it is a completed ad impression with viewability confirmed; for a marketplace, a listing fee paid by the other side. Teams that assume monetisation means transaction conclude free products have no monetisation funnel, then miss ad-load changes quietly destroying retention.

The same person triggers all three actions repeatedly. ARM is three counters, not three life stages stamped once. The tell is language: "our retained users" spoken as a fixed segment rather than a rate recomputed each period. A user can be at once a retention success and a monetisation failure; averaging them into a health score destroys the information.

An action can be right and still be gameable. Bandobast's seat measure was well instrumented, correctly windowed and wholly uncorrelated with renewal. The diagnostic is not whether an action is well defined but whether it predicts money: regress it against renewal or twelve-month contribution before putting it on a wall.

Retention interventions need a holdout and a horizon longer than their own window. A day-nine reminder that lifts fourteen-day retention nine points and leaves ninety-day orders unchanged has moved the metric, not the business. The tell is a lift appearing exactly at the measurement boundary and vanishing at twice that horizon.

Acquisition mix change masquerades as product change. When a channel with different user quality enters the mix, blended retention falls even though retention improved within every channel — the aggregation paradox at its most expensive. Hold mix constant across periods, or compare channel by channel.

Involuntary churn is a payments problem in a product costume. A large share of subscription cancellations in Indian consumer products begin as failed debits, not decisions. The tell is a cancellation spike aligned to a calendar date rather than a usage pattern — the first of the month, the day after a tokenisation deadline. Reading it as dissatisfaction produces a roadmap aimed at billing retry logic.

7. How it changes by product type and stage

In consumer products all three actions occur within days; the risk is that acquisition, being the most fundable and visible, absorbs attention it has not earned. In B2B and enterprise the ordering inverts, monetisation precedes usage, and the three actions belong to three functions on quarterly cadences; the meaningful retention action is almost never login-based and almost always workflow-share-based. In platforms and marketplaces ARM runs twice with a lag between ledgers, and the constraint side determines everything. In hardware the economics compress into attach rate and consumable renewal, and in AI products the framework needs an explicit cost term per retained user.

The difference is overstated in one place: the five fixings do not vary by product type or stage. Stage changes only granularity and automation — an early team reviews three numbers monthly; a mature one runs the same three per city, language, channel and cohort, with alerting instead of staring. Teams mistake "we are early" for permission to skip the fixings, the one thing stage never licenses.

8. Three worked examples

Ankahi's paywall: the test that answered the wrong question

Rukmini's team modelled a 1,00,000-install Marathi cohort over twelve months rather than reading the thirty-day number. Under the control, 22,000 were retained at day 30, each generating about ₹7 of ad margin per active month at a free-listener retention of 0.78 — 4.32 expected active months — while 2.1% started trials, converting to 462 subscribers at ₹110 net who retained at 0.94 for 8.74 paying months. Under the paywall, retention fell to 16,000, ad margin to ₹4.83, subscribers rose to 864.

A change described as 2.5x was, correctly measured, indistinguishable from neutral — a useful finding, because the decision then turns on grounds the test never measured: cash timing, exposure to a soft programmatic ad market, and the fact that a smaller free base seeds fewer word-of-mouth installs.

Bandobast: changing the action, not the number

Arvind's team abandoned weekly active seats for a workflow-share measure: "in a given month, at least 60% of the account's distributor order value arrived through the portal". Re-cut against twelve-month outcomes, it separated customers the old measure never had.

The asymmetry is specific: a definition error does not produce one wrong decision, it retroactively invalidates every comparison crossing the change, so its cost scales with the length of history the team was relying on.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The live disagreement is about where a marginal rupee goes, and both positions are held by serious people with evidence.

Retention-first, at its strongest: retention is the only ARM rate appearing twice in the value equation — once as a rate, again inside the survival multiplier — so its returns are convex while acquisition's are linear. The evidence is the arithmetic in Figure 2 and the observation that products whose retention curves never flatten have never been rescued by acquisition spend. It would be wrong if retention were a fixed property of the category rather than something a team can move.

Penetration-first, at its strongest: that condition is very often what obtains. Ehrenberg-Bass's cross-category work finds buying frequencies stably distributed, brand growth driven overwhelmingly by adding light buyers, and loyalty differences between competing brands far smaller than marketing lore claims. On this reading most retention programmes reallocate behaviour that would have happened anyway. It would be wrong if switching costs, data accumulation and habit formation make software loyalty manipulable in ways a biscuit brand's is not.

The evidence has not settled this, because almost all published retention-improvement results come from companies already growing, with acquisition mix moving at the same time. Two questions stay open: whether the multiplicative model should give way to hazard models assuming no stages at all, and whether ARM's vocabulary survives products where the user never visits — agentic software acting on a schedule, where "returned" has no observable moment.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied ARM produces a three-box diagram and three rates. Someone who has internalised it differs in four observable ways. They ask for the event name before the number, and will not discuss a rate whose identity grain and window have not been stated in the same sentence. They keep a definitions change log and treat a change during a live experiment as an incident, not an improvement. They can say which stage is binding today, what one point costs at each stage, and what evidence would make a different stage binding next quarter — the last being the part nobody does. And they are comfortable reporting that a well-run test was value-neutral, because the alternative is a company that only learns things which flatter it.

12. What they decided

On 30 September, Rukmini recommended against the national rollout and proposed something narrower: keep the ad-supported model, wall only completed series older than ninety days, and fund Sneha's team in Indore to attack subscriber retention and trial conversion — the two cheapest points in Exhibit D. The test had been honestly run and returned a null result; a 4.9% edge did not justify shrinking the free base that seeded word of mouth; and ₹5 lakh at the bottom of the funnel bought more than ₹35 lakh at the top. The chief executive was unenthusiastic; the proposal passed because Rukmini could put a number on the alternative.

Arvind retired weekly active seats within a fortnight, replaced it with portal share of distributor order value, and rebuilt the implementation exit criterion around the 60% threshold. One further change cost nothing: every ARM action acquired a named owner, a cadence and a written decision, and any definition change required Prachi's sign-off and appeared in a log. Bandobast's net revenue retention reached 112% by the following March — short of the board's 120%, and the first number in three years Arvind believed.

Discussion questions.

1. Rukmini treated a 4.9% twelve-month edge as indistinguishable from zero. What would have to be true of the variance of her retention estimate, and of Ankahi's cash position, for the paywall to be right anyway?

2. Bandobast's old retention action was well instrumented and useless. What is the cheapest test to run, before adopting an action, to learn whether it predicts money — and why do so few companies run it?

3. Bindu's recovery made every chart look worse before it looked better. How should a product leader sequence and communicate a definition change that will temporarily make the company appear to be shrinking?

13. Going deeper

  1. GAME framework — the parent structure ARM sits inside, supplying the goal and evaluation steps that decide whether an action was worth naming.
  2. Pirate metrics (AARRR) — splits ARM's first bucket into acquisition and activation and adds referral, where Rukmini's word-of-mouth argument becomes measurable rather than rhetorical.
  3. Constructing a funnel — turns three buckets into a diagram with a conversion rate on every edge, the only way to attribute a shortfall to a stage.
  4. Defining activation (the aha moment) — the missing action between acquisition and retention, and the usual explanation for a healthy acquisition rate that produces nothing.
  5. What makes a good metric — criteria that would have disqualified Bandobast's seat measure before it cost three years.
  6. Vanity vs actionable metrics — the discipline behind Bindu's redefinition: what a giveaway can satisfy is not measuring the business.
  7. Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — why a rate without its count misleads, and when a proxy action is legitimate.
  8. North Star metric — the case for a single measure above the ARM ledger, and the well-founded objections to it.
  9. Attention, transaction, productivity games — which game a product plays determines which ARM action is structurally binding, before any data arrives.
  10. Breadth × depth × frequency — opens the retention action itself, separating how many users return from how deeply and how often.

Ghar Seva: Twelve Crore Before Diwali

Gurugram, 12 September 2025. A head of product has ₹12 crore, five weeks, and three teams each certain the money belongs to them.

1. Friday evening, Sector 44

The monsoon had broken over Gurugram by six o'clock, and Meenal Deshmukh could hear the water on the windows of the eighth-floor conference room where she had spent most of the day. On the table in front of her were three one-page proposals, each asking for the whole of the ₹12 crore festive budget the board had approved for the quarter. Meenal was head of product at Ghar Seva Technologies, a seven-year-old home-services company that sent trained professionals to customers' homes for salon services, appliance repair, deep cleaning and pest control across eleven Indian cities and, since 2024, Dubai.

The budget had to be committed by 17 October, three days before Dhanteras, because the media buys and the professional-hiring pipeline both needed five weeks of lead time. Ghar Seva's chief executive had asked for a single recommendation with a single number attached to it. What made the ask uncomfortable was that all three proposals were supported by real data, and the data did not agree about what Ghar Seva's problem was.

2. Ghar Seva Technologies

Ghar Seva had been founded in 2018 by two IIT Delhi graduates who had noticed that the market for household services in Indian cities ran entirely on the informal recommendations of neighbours and building watchmen. The company recruited electricians, beauticians, cleaners and technicians, trained them at centres in Gurugram, Pune and Hyderabad, put them in uniforms with a ₹15 lakh-a-year earnings promise for the best performers, and sold their time through an app with fixed prices and a rating system.

By August 2025 the company was doing an annualised gross transaction value of about ₹2,100 crore, of which it kept roughly 26 percent as revenue. It had 8.4 million app installs, 1.6 million customers who had completed at least one booking, and 41,000 active professionals. Its competition came from several directions at once: Urban Company in the organised segment, listings on Justdial and neighbourhood WhatsApp groups in the unorganised one, and increasingly the services tabs inside Flipkart and Paytm, both of which had offered Ghar Seva co-marketing slots for the festive season. Payments ran almost entirely on UPI through a Razorpay integration; the company had registered as a data fiduciary under the DPDP Act in early 2025 and had spent four months rebuilding its consent flows as a result.

The team had grown outward from Gurugram. The core engineering group sat in Bengaluru and Pune; the design lead, Lena Brandt, worked from Berlin and joined Indian stand-ups at six in the morning her time; the data science function had been built around Divya Balakrishnan in Toronto, hired in 2023 when Ghar Seva could not match Bengaluru salary bands for senior analysts; Kavitha Rangan ran customer success from Singapore, covering both the Indian night shift and the Dubai business; and Arjun Pillai, in New Jersey, sold a facilities-management version of the platform to property companies, with one large contract in Dubai worth ₹9.4 crore a year.

3. The situation

The trouble had started in June, when Ghar Seva's monthly revenue growth slowed to 2 percent after eleven months averaging 7 percent. Installs had not slowed; they had risen, helped by a cricket-season campaign. What had changed was somewhere in the middle, and for most of July nobody could say where, because Ghar Seva's weekly review tracked three numbers — installs, monthly transacting customers, and revenue — with nothing between them.

In August, Divya rebuilt the company's reporting around user actions rather than user states. She defined three actions and computed them by monthly cohort: a customer was acquired when a first booking was completed and rated, retained when a second booking was completed within 60 days of the first, and monetised when she bought Ghar Seva Plus, the ₹999 annual membership the company had soft-launched in Bengaluru and Hyderabad in April, which gave 10 percent off every booking and priority slots on weekends.

Her cohort tables, which became Exhibit 1, showed something the old dashboard had hidden entirely. Acquisition was healthy and improving. The second-booking rate — the retention action — had fallen from 34 percent to 27 percent over four cohorts. And the membership had converted well, but almost all of its buyers came from the small group of customers who had already made a second booking; among customers who bought Plus before their second booking, three in five never booked again and a fifth asked for a refund.

From Singapore, Kavitha read the same fall differently. Her team's tickets pointed at supply: in the cities where the second-booking rate had dropped furthest, the share of bookings assigned to a professional with fewer than ten completed jobs had risen from 18 percent to 33 percent, because hiring had been accelerated to meet the install surge. Lena, in Berlin, had a third reading — that the rebuilt DPDP consent flow, which now asked for notification permission in a separate step, had cut the share of customers reachable by a rebooking reminder from 71 percent to 48 percent.

Figure 1 sets out the sequence of decisions that produced the September stand-off, together with where in the world each of the three readings was being formed. Meenal's own view, by the second week of September, was that the three explanations were not competing theories so much as three different answers to a question the company had never asked in the first place: which actions, exactly, is Ghar Seva trying to get a customer to take?

4. The people

Farhan Qureshi, VP Growth, Bengaluru. Farhan had the Flipkart and Paytm festive slots on hold until 17 October and a blended cost per install of ₹41, the lowest Ghar Seva had ever seen. His proposal asked for the full ₹12 crore to buy roughly 29 lakh installs during the festive window, arguing that Diwali is when Indian households clean, repaint and repair, and that a customer acquired in October behaves better for the next year than one acquired in June. His quarterly incentive was tied to new transacting customers.

Divya Balakrishnan, Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Divya's proposal asked for ₹12 crore against the retention action: a ₹250 credit released on a second booking made within 45 days, a guarantee that a repeat customer would be assigned a professional with at least twenty completed jobs, and the engineering work in Pune to make both possible. Her memo contained one sentence that Meenal had underlined twice: "Every rate we report divides by installs, which is why the only number that looks bad is the one nobody owns."

Sandeep Malhotra, CFO, Gurugram. Sandeep wanted the membership pushed hard and nationally. His reasoning was cash: ₹999 collected in October is cash in October, it improves the working-capital position before the Series D conversations in February, and deferred revenue recognised over twelve months smooths the revenue line the board watches. He was aware of the refund rate and considered it a support problem rather than a product one.

Kavitha Rangan, Head of Customer Success, Singapore. Kavitha wanted the money spent on professionals, not customers — training throughput, a higher guaranteed weekly payout for the festive period, and a cap on how many new professionals could be onboarded per city per month. She had told Meenal privately that a big October install push with the current supply mix would produce the worst customer experience in the company's history, and that her Dubai contract's service-level clauses gave her no room for it.

6. The options

Option A: buy the festival. Commit the ₹12 crore to Farhan's plan — the Flipkart and Paytm co-marketing slots, performance media, and a Dhanteras offer. At ₹41 per install this buys roughly 29 lakh installs; at the July cohort's rates it yields about 6.1 lakh first bookings and, at 27 percent, 1.65 lakh second bookings. The upside is scale at the cheapest install price the company has seen and a defensible growth number for the Series D. The cost is that Exhibit 1's trend is a trend: if the retention action keeps falling as volume rises, Ghar Seva spends ₹12 crore to make its contribution per thousand installs worse, and Kavitha's supply warning suggests that is the likely direction.

Option B: fix the second booking. Commit the money to Divya's and Kavitha's combined plan: the ₹250 second-booking credit, the experienced-professional guarantee for repeat customers, a per-city cap on new professional onboarding, a higher festive payout to retain good professionals, and the Pune engineering work plus a Berlin redesign of the notification-consent step. The upside is that every point of second-booking rate multiplies the entire acquired population and compounds into the following year. The cost is that almost none of the spend produces a visible number before December, the install volume the board expects will not appear, and a ₹250 credit given at scale has a real cash cost with no certainty that it buys a habit rather than a discount.

Option C: sell the membership. Commit the money to a national Ghar Seva Plus launch: festive pricing at ₹749, in-app placement at the end of every first booking, and a media campaign. The upside is immediate cash, a recurring-revenue line for the Series D, and a mechanism that by construction increases booking frequency among members. The cost is the composition risk Exhibit 3 exposes: a national push at the end of the first booking sells mostly to the segment worth ₹402, and 21 percent of them will ask for their money back in a quarter when customer success is already stretched.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, state in one sentence each what Ghar Seva's acquisition, retention and monetisation actions are, and which of the three is actually deteriorating. Why did the company's old dashboard — installs, monthly transacting customers, revenue — make this invisible for two months?

2. Exhibit 2 is a correlation across six cities, and Exhibit 3 is a split of a pilot that was not randomised. What would you want to know before treating either as evidence for a ₹12 crore decision, and what could Ghar Seva measure in the five weeks it has?

3. Farhan's incentive is tied to new transacting customers and Sandeep's to cash collected this quarter. How much of the disagreement in this case is a disagreement about facts, and how much is a disagreement about which stage each executive is paid to move?

4. What should Meenal recommend on 17 October, and what single number should she ask the board to judge her by for the next four quarters? Defend your number against the objection that it will make the festive quarter look worse than Option A would.

8. A note for the learner

This case is a test of whether a reader can separate three actions that a single revenue line blends together. The lens is simple: name the action a customer takes to become a user, the action she takes to become a returning user, and the action she takes to become revenue; measure each against the population that cleared the stage before it; and then ask which action, if moved, moves the money most. Ghar Seva's three proposals are not three strategies. They are three stages of one chain, each championed by the executive who owns it, and the chain has exactly one weak link.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. It identifies the retention action — a second booking within 60 days — as the deteriorating stage, and notices that the deterioration was hidden because every rate on the old dashboard used installs as its denominator. It treats Exhibit 3 as evidence about sequence rather than about membership: the same product is worth ₹2,910 or ₹402 depending on which action the customer has already taken, so the monetisation action should be gated behind the retention action rather than placed before it. And it treats Exhibit 2 with appropriate suspicion — six cities, confounded by where the install spend went — while conceding that supply quality and repeat rate are plausibly linked and cheap to test.

One defensible path: Meenal commits roughly ₹8.5 crore to Option B, keeps about ₹2.5 crore of Farhan's festive spend but restricts it to the four cities where the inexperienced-professional share is below 25 percent, and spends the remaining ₹1 crore launching Plus at ₹749 only to customers who have completed a second booking, measured as a controlled test against a holdout. She proposes as her board metric second-booking customers per 1,000 installs — 56.7 for the July cohort against 61.2 in March — because it cannot be improved by buying cheaper installs or by selling memberships to customers who will refund them, and it falls if either the acquisition action or the retention action degrades.

The reasoning is that Ghar Seva's cheapest available growth is not in the 29 lakh installs it has not yet bought but in the 1.6 lakh acquired customers a quarter it is currently losing between the first booking and the second. A five-point recovery in the second-booking rate is worth roughly 11,000 additional retained customers per monthly cohort at no acquisition cost, and Exhibit 3 says each of those is the only kind of customer to whom the membership can be sold profitably. Option A is not wrong so much as premature: it multiplies a funnel that is leaking at the stage nobody owns.

Arthveda Money: Sixty-Two Lakh Activations

Mumbai, Sunday 8 February 2026, 11.40 p.m. The board meets at nine. Every number in the pre-read is defensible, and no two of them describe the same company.

1. The night before

The office on the eighth floor of a converted mill building in Lower Parel had emptied by nine, and Nandini Iyer had the floor to herself except for the security guard, who had brought her a second cup of tea without being asked. She was forty-one, had been Arthveda Money's chief product officer for two years and eight months, and had spent the evening trying to reconcile two slides that she was fairly sure could not be reconciled.

The first slide, prepared by the growth team, said that Arthveda had activated 62.1 lakh users since April 2024 and was therefore on course to clear the 50-lakh milestone in its agreement with Sahyog Digital Partners by 31 March, releasing the final ₹45 crore tranche of a ₹120 crore strategic investment. The second slide, prepared in Toronto, said that 9.4 lakh users had ever made a voluntary investment of ₹500 or more, that 3.1 lakh still had a live auto-debit mandate ninety days after signing up, and that the median portfolio across the entire activated base was ₹340.

Both slides were correct. They differed because the word "activated" meant one thing in a contract signed in 2023 and a different thing in a product-analytics warehouse rebuilt in 2025, and because nobody had ever been asked to choose between the two definitions in a room where the chief executive and the Sahyog nominee were both present.

Nandini's problem on Monday was narrower and harder than the philosophical one. Arthveda had ₹34 crore of cash, a fourteen-month runway on current burn, eleven engineers in Pune who were fully committed until 30 April to a mandated change in how recurring e-mandates were authenticated, a designer in Berlin on a notice period, and a board that had asked for "one number we can hold the product organisation to for FY27". She had written four versions of the slide that answered that question and deleted all four. At 11.40 p.m. she opened a fifth.

2. How Arthveda got here

Arthveda Money was founded in 2019 in Mumbai by Nandini's co-founder and chief executive, Rohit Bakshi, and a former mutual-fund distribution head, on a premise that was unfashionable at the time and obvious by 2024: that the ninety-odd million Indians who had a UPI handle but no investment account would not be reached by an app that asked them to choose between eleven hundred mutual fund schemes. Arthveda's answer was Bachat Auto — a feature that rounded up every UPI payment the user made to the next ₹10 and swept the difference, once a week, into a portfolio of digital gold and two index funds. The average sweep was ₹47.

The company registered as a mutual fund distributor with AMFI, held a SEBI registration for its execution-only platform activity, and earned money three ways: trail commission on assets it had distributed, a ₹299-a-year subscription called Arthveda Pro that removed a ₹9 per-sweep fee and added goal-tracking, and float on money in transit. By January 2026 it had 1.42 crore app installs, ₹1,840 crore of assets under distribution, and revenue of ₹61 crore annualised.

The decision that constrains everything in this case was taken in August 2023. Arthveda needed capital and distribution; Sahyog Digital Partners, the consumer-internet arm of a large Indian industrial group, needed a financial-services product to put in front of the 19 crore users of its telecom and retail properties. The deal was ₹120 crore in three tranches, the third of which — ₹45 crore — was contingent on Arthveda delivering 50 lakh "Activated Users" by 31 March 2026, with Sahyog reimbursing acquisition costs up to ₹180 per activated user.

Clause 7.3(b) of the agreement defined an Activated User as "a unique individual who has completed KYC verification and executed at least one investment transaction of not less than ₹100 through the Platform." The clause had been drafted by lawyers in ten minutes at the end of a long negotiation, and in 2023 it had seemed a reasonable proxy for a customer. Rohit had approved it. So had Nandini, who remembered thinking that ₹100 was a low bar and that it would be embarrassing to argue for a lower one.

3. The industry around it

By early 2026 the Indian retail-investing market had four distinct shapes of competitor, and Arthveda sat awkwardly between them. Zerodha and Groww dominated the self-directed segment with deep product and very low customer acquisition costs built on brand and content. Paytm Money and PhonePe's wealth offerings had distribution Arthveda could not match. A cohort of round-up and micro-savings apps — Jar most visibly — was competing for exactly Arthveda's user and had driven cost per KYC-complete user from ₹96 in 2023 to about ₹230 by the end of 2025. And the asset management companies themselves had begun to build direct apps that paid no distribution commission at all.

Three regulatory and macro currents bore directly on the decision in front of Nandini. First, the Reserve Bank of India's framework for recurring e-mandates, operated through NPCI's UPI AutoPay rails, required pre-debit notification and periodic re-authentication; a revision effective 1 May 2026 was the work occupying the Pune engineers. Second, SEBI had published a consultation paper in November 2025 on disclosure and commission practices for execution-only platforms; nobody in the industry expected commissions to be abolished, but everybody was modelling a scenario in which trail revenue per rupee of assets fell by a fifth. Third, the DPDP Act's consent architecture had, since Arthveda's compliance rebuild in mid-2025, made it materially harder to reach a dormant user: the share of the base that had granted notification consent after the rebuild was 44 percent, against 78 percent before it.

Arthveda also had exposure outside India, and it mattered more than its size suggested. In November 2025 the company had begun a pilot with Al Manzil Exchange, a Dubai remittance house, offering NRI customers a version of Bachat Auto that swept a share of each remittance into an Indian portfolio. Eleven weeks in, the pilot had 4,100 users, an average first investment of ₹9,400, and a ninety-day mandate survival rate that Toronto had refused to report on the grounds that ninety days had not yet elapsed. Arjun Pillai, Arthveda's sales head in New Jersey, had two US-based Indian-diaspora employer channels in his pipeline and a view about where the company's future revenue was.

4. The situation in detail

The timeline matters because at each point the company believed something that later turned out to be wrong.

April 2024. Arthveda launched a Sahyog-funded acquisition programme: a ₹100 investment credit for any new user who completed KYC and made a first investment of ₹100. The credit cost Arthveda nothing net of the Sahyog reimbursement, and it produced activations at a rate nobody had seen before — 4.1 lakh in the first full month. The belief at the time was that the credit was buying customers cheaply. The growth team's dashboard showed activation cost of ₹186, comfortably under the ₹180 reimbursement once one netted off the credit itself, which finance treated as a marketing expense and growth treated as a pass-through.

September 2024. The first cohort analysis of the programme, run by a contractor, showed 90-day retention of 41 percent, which was above the company's historical average. The belief was that the programme was working. What has since turned out to be wrong is the measurement: the contractor had defined a retained user as one who opened the app in the ninetieth day window, and because the app sent a weekly portfolio notification that opened the app when tapped, "retention" was partly a measure of notification delivery. Nobody noticed until the DPDP consent rebuild cut notification reach and the same metric fell 24 points in six weeks without any change in investing behaviour.

March 2025. Arthveda crossed 30 lakh activations and raised its FY26 revenue guidance on the strength of it. The belief was that assets under distribution would follow users with a lag. They did not follow at the assumed rate: the March 2025 board deck modelled ₹1,100 of assets per activated user by month twelve, and the realised figure for the April–June 2024 cohorts was ₹390.

August 2025. Arthveda migrated from its original analytics implementation to a warehouse-native event pipeline, a project run by Pune and Toronto together. The migration renamed and consolidated events. Among other things, the old event investment_made had fired both for a user-initiated investment and for an automated round-up sweep; the new taxonomy split these into investment_voluntary and sweep_executed. This split is the reason the second slide in Nandini's pre-read exists at all — and it is also why no cohort before August 2025 can be compared to one after it on the voluntary-investment measure, a caveat that appears in a footnote on page 31 of the pre-read and nowhere else.

November 2025. Divya Krishnan in Toronto circulated an analysis showing that the single strongest predictor of a user's twelve-month asset balance was neither the first investment nor app-open frequency but whether the user's auto-debit mandate was still live at day 90. Mandate survival explained more variance than every other candidate action combined. The finding was received well and then complicated: mandate survival varied by sponsor bank from 71 percent to 34 percent, for reasons — bank-side re-authentication flows, SMS delivery, debit-failure handling — that had nothing to do with Arthveda's product.

January 2026. Two things happened in the same week. 8. The options as Nandini sees them

By eleven o'clock she had reduced her fifth draft to three options, written on the whiteboard in her own handwriting, and she was uneasily aware that all three took the existing funnel as given.

The first is to finish the quarter. Give Farid the affiliate budget, clear 50 lakh activations by 31 March, bank the ₹45 crore, and propose a definitional change for FY27 in April, when Vikram has said he would be willing to discuss it and when a longer channel arrangement might be on the table. The cost is twelve lakh more users acquired on a journey that Kavitha says produces people who do not know they are customers, roughly ₹28 crore of net spend on the finance basis of Exhibit 2, and a base that Exhibit 5 suggests is 58 percent contribution-negative.

The second is to change the company's retention action now: adopt mandate-live-at-day-90 as the FY27 metric, rebuild onboarding around Lena's goal-first flow before she leaves, accept a lower first-investment rate, and tell the board that Arthveda will miss clause 7.3(b) and forgo the tranche. The cost is the ₹45 crore, the Series D narrative Rohit has already told investors, and a metric that Exhibit 3 shows is half determined by which bank the user uses. The benefit is that the company would for the first time be measuring something a user does that has money behind it.

The third is to move the company's centre of gravity to monetisation and to the NRI corridor: push paid Pro to the domestic base, scale the Al Manzil pilot, give Arjun the two US employer channels, and let the domestic round-up base run at maintenance. The cost is that Exhibit 6 rests on 4,100 users and eleven weeks, that the DPDP data-residency question Arjun has not raised could stop the employer channels entirely, and that scaling a corridor requires the same eleven Pune engineers who are committed to the e-mandate work until 30 April.

What she kept circling back to, and what did not fit on the whiteboard, was a suspicion that the three options shared a premise. Each assumed that Arthveda had one funnel with one user. Exhibit 5's four segments behave like four different products; Exhibit 4's subscriber count contains a monetisation action performed by a partner rather than a person; Exhibit 6 describes a user whose first action is a remittance, not an investment. It was possible that the company's real problem was not which of three stages to fund but that it had been running three businesses through one set of definitions for twenty-two months, and that any metric chosen for the whole would be wrong for each part. She did not know what to do with that thought before nine o'clock.
